# Plot theme matching the light lecture template
theme_slides <- function(base_size = 15) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA),
      panel.grid       = element_line(colour = "#00000018"),
      text             = element_text(colour = "#222222"),
      axis.text        = element_text(colour = "#555555")
    )
}

# --- The standard genetic code, built from first principles -----------------
bases   <- c("T", "C", "A", "G")
codons  <- paste0(rep(bases, each = 16), rep(rep(bases, each = 4), 4), rep(bases, 16))
aminos  <- strsplit("FFLLSSSSYY**CC*WLLLLPPPPHHQQRRRRIIIMTTTTNNKKSSRRVVVVAAAADDEEGGGG", "")[[1]]
gencode <- setNames(aminos, codons)

translate_dna <- function(s) {
  s  <- toupper(gsub("[^ACGTacgt]", "", s))
  cs <- substring(s, seq(1, nchar(s) - 2, 3), seq(3, nchar(s), 3))
  paste(gencode[cs], collapse = "")
}

# --- Primer arithmetic ------------------------------------------------------
gc_pct <- function(x) {
  v <- strsplit(toupper(x), "")[[1]]
  round(100 * sum(v %in% c("G", "C")) / sum(v %in% c("A", "C", "G", "T")), 1)
}

tm_wallace <- function(x) {
  v <- strsplit(toupper(x), "")[[1]]
  2 * sum(v %in% c("A", "T")) + 4 * sum(v %in% c("G", "C"))
}

---

## Today we cover

::: {.incremental}
1. **DNA and RNA** — building blocks, base pairing, the double helix, and RNA's many jobs;
2. **The genetic code** — codons, redundancy, synonymous and non-synonymous change;
3. **Proteins** — amino acids, four levels of structure, ribosomes at work;
4. **Genomes** — size, gene number, chromatin packing, and epigenetic marks;
5. **Mutation and replication** — transitions, transversions, and the modes of genetic innovation;
6. **The first toolkit** — PCR, melting temperature, electrophoresis, Sanger sequencing;
7. **Molecular ecology** — from allozymes to SNPs, and the rRNA tree of life.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two halves: the molecules first, then what ecologists do with them. Everything after PCR is method; everything before it is why the method works.
:::

---

# Basics of molecular biology

DNA · RNA · proteins · genomes

---

## DNA — the building blocks

![](/assets/code_of_life/p05_1.jpg){height="430px"}

::: {.credit}
(A) nucleotide · (B) DNA strand · (C) templated polymerisation · (D) double-stranded DNA · (E) the double helix
:::

---

## Nucleotide chemistry

![](/assets/code_of_life/p06_1.jpg){height="380px"}

::: {.incremental}
- **Purines** — adenine, guanine — two rings;
- **Pyrimidines** — cytosine, thymine (DNA), uracil (RNA) — one ring;
- sugar + base = **nucleoside**; add phosphates = **nucleotide**.
:::

---

## Complementary base pairs

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p07_1.jpg){height="420px"}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
The shapes and chemistry of the bases allow hydrogen bonds to form efficiently **only**:

- between **A and T** — two hydrogen bonds;
- between **G and C** — three hydrogen bonds.

The bases can pair this way only if the two polynucleotide chains are **antiparallel**.

::: {.callout-note}
Three bonds vs two is the whole reason GC-rich DNA melts at a higher temperature — remember this when we reach primers and probes.
:::
:::
:::

---

## The double helix

![](/assets/code_of_life/p08_1.jpg){height="450px"}

::: {.credit}
Major and minor grooves · 2 nm diameter · 0.34 nm rise per base pair · phosphodiester backbone
:::

---

## RNA vs DNA — and the types of RNA

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p09_1.jpg)

**(a)** ribose instead of deoxyribose
**(b)** uracil in place of thymine
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p09_2.jpg)

Messenger (mRNA) · ribosomal (rRNA) · transfer (tRNA)
:::
:::

---

## RNA does more than carry messages {.scrollable}

![](/assets/code_of_life/p10_1.jpg){height="420px"}

::: {.credit}
siRNA, miRNA, and piRNA pathways — Großhans & Filipowicz, *Nature* 2008
:::

---

## The conformation of RNA molecules

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p11_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**(A)** Nucleotide pairing between different regions of the *same* RNA chain gives the molecule a distinctive shape.

**(B)** The three-dimensional structure of a real RNA — from hepatitis delta virus — that **catalyses** RNA strand cleavage.

The blue ribbon is the sugar–phosphate backbone; the bars are base pairs.
:::
:::

---

## Ribosomal RNA — the workhorse marker

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p12_1.jpg){height="400px"}

::: {.credit}
*Thermus thermophilus* small-subunit rRNA
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p12_2.jpg)

The **16S rRNA** gene is ~1600 bp long and contains **nine hypervariable regions** (V1–V9) of differing conservation.

::: {.callout-tip}
Conserved stretches give you primer sites; variable stretches give you taxonomic signal. Every 16S amplicon study is a choice about which V-regions to read.
:::
:::
:::

---

## Transfer RNA

![](/assets/code_of_life/p13_1.jpg){height="400px"}

**(A)** A tRNA specific for tryptophan: the amino acid sits on one end, the **anticodon** (CCA end shown) on the other, recognising the tryptophan codon in mRNA. **(B)** Its three-dimensional structure.

---

## The genetic code

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p14_1.jpg){height="420px"}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.incremental}
- A substitution that does **not** change the amino acid — thanks to redundancy — is **synonymous** (same-sense, silent);
- a **non-synonymous** substitution corrupts the original specification of the codon;
- **mis-sense** — the codon now specifies a different amino acid;
- **non-sense** — the codon becomes a stop codon.
:::
:::
:::

---

## The code, in R

```{r}
#| label: gencode
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
#| classes: fragment

bases   <- c("T", "C", "A", "G")
codons  <- paste0(rep(bases, each = 16), rep(rep(bases, each = 4), 4), rep(bases, 16))
aminos  <- strsplit("FFLLSSSSYY**CC*WLLLLPPPPHHQQRRRRIIIMTTTTNNKKSSRRVVVVAAAADDEEGGGG", "")[[1]]
gencode <- setNames(aminos, codons)

# 64 codons, 20 amino acids, 3 stops
table(gencode) |> sort(decreasing = TRUE) |> head(6)

translate_dna("ATG GCT TGG AAA TAA")
```

::: {.callout-note}
Six codons for leucine and serine, one for methionine and tryptophan. That imbalance is what "redundancy" means in practice — and why synonymous sites accumulate change almost freely.
:::

---

## Recoding a genome — a virus-resistant organism

![](/assets/code_of_life/p15_1.jpg){height="400px"}

Reassign the redundant codons, delete the matching tRNAs, and an invading phage can no longer translate its own proteins in the host.

---

## Amino acids and optical isomers

![](/assets/code_of_life/p16_1.jpg){height="330px"}

The α-carbon is asymmetric, so amino acids come as two mirror images (L and D). **Proteins consist exclusively of L-amino acids.**

---

## Families of amino acids {.scrollable}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p17_1.jpg){height="430px"}
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
The 20 common amino acids are grouped by their **side chains**:

- acidic
- basic
- uncharged polar
- nonpolar

Each has a three-letter and a one-letter abbreviation — alanine = Ala = A.

![](/assets/code_of_life/p17_2.jpg)
:::
:::

---

## Protein structure

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p18_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p18_2.jpg){height="230px"}
:::
:::

- **primary** — the precise order of amino acids in the chain;
- **secondary** — weak interactions, mostly hydrogen bonding;
- **tertiary** — folding in three dimensions (hydrophobic interactions; sometimes disulphide bridges between two Cys);
- **quaternary** — two or more tertiary structures forming one functional protein.

---

## Ribosome structure

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p19_1.jpg){height="360px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
The ribosome has a **small** and a **large** subunit.

Subunit and rRNA sizes are given as a **sedimentation coefficient** *S* (Svedberg), which depends on relative molecular mass *and* shape.

::: {.callout-warning}
S values do not add up: 30S + 50S = **70S**, not 80S. Sedimentation is not mass.
:::
:::
:::

---

## Coding genes (animals)

![](/assets/code_of_life/p20_1.jpg){height="420px"}

::: {.credit}
Hulley J. & Holland P., *Nature* 2004 — vertebrates converge on ~20,000–25,000 protein-coding genes, and so do *Ciona* and *C. elegans*
:::

---

## DNA → RNA → proteins

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p21_1.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p21_2.jpg)

Life as an **autocatalytic process**: polynucleotides carry the *sequence information*, proteins provide the *catalytic function*, and together — through a complex set of chemical reactions — they make more of both.
:::
:::

---

## The ribosome at work

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p22_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p22_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p22_3.jpg)
:::
:::

The ribosome moves along the mRNA, capturing tRNAs that match the codons and joining their amino acids into a protein chain. **The mRNA specifies the sequence of amino acids.**

---

## Controlling gene read-out by environmental signals {.scrollable}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p23_1.jpg){height="430px"}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
Regulatory DNA lets gene expression be controlled by **regulatory proteins** (e.g. transcription factors) — which are themselves the products of other genes.

The signal may, for example, trigger attachment of a **phosphate group** to the regulatory protein, altering its chemical properties:

![](/assets/code_of_life/p23_2.jpg)
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the hinge between molecular biology and ecology: the environment is not just a selective filter, it is an input to the expression machinery on a timescale of minutes.
:::

## Genome sizes compared

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p26_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
The human genome contains **1000×** as many nucleotide pairs as a typical bacterium, **20×** as many genes, and about **10,000×** as much noncoding DNA.

~98.5% of the human genome is noncoding, against 11% of *E. coli*.
:::
:::

## Packing of the chromatin fibre

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p27_1.jpg){height="420px"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p27_2.jpg)

![](/assets/code_of_life/p27_3.jpg)

::: {.credit}
2 nm double helix → nucleosomes → 30 nm fibre → 300 nm loops → 700 nm → 1400 nm mitotic chromosome
:::
:::

## Euchromatin and heterochromatin

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p27_4.jpg){height="380px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p28_1.jpg)

Modification of DNA and histone proteins:

- **methylation** packs nucleosomes tightly — DNA inaccessible, gene inactive;
- **acetylation** loosens the packing — DNA accessible, gene active.
:::
:::

---

## Human chromosomes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p29_1.jpg){height="420px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p29_2.jpg){height="420px"}
:::
:::

::: {.credit}
Chromosome 22: ~48 × 10⁶ bp → 10% of an arm ≈ 40 genes → 1% ≈ 4 genes → one gene of 3.4 × 10⁴ bp
:::

## Mutations

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p30_1.jpg)

Insertion · inversion
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p30_2.jpg)

Substitution · deletion
:::
:::

---

## Transitions and transversions

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p31_1.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Transitions** — purine ↔ purine (A↔G) or pyrimidine ↔ pyrimidine (C↔T): bases of similar shape;
- **Transversions** — purine ↔ pyrimidine: one-ring for two-ring.

There are **twice as many possible** transversions, yet transitions are generated **more often**. Transitions are also less likely to change the amino acid (wobble), so they persist as silent substitutions — the SNPs we later genotype.
:::
:::

---

## Ti/Tv, in R

```{r}
#| label: titv
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

purines <- c("A", "G")

classify_sub <- function(from, to) {
  ifelse(from == to, "same",
    ifelse((from %in% purines) == (to %in% purines), "transition", "transversion"))
}

ref <- strsplit("ACGTTGCAAGGTCCATGAC", "")[[1]]
alt <- strsplit("ATGTTAGAAAGTACGTGAC", "")[[1]]

subs <- data.frame(pos = seq_along(ref), ref, alt, type = classify_sub(ref, alt)) |>
  filter(type != "same")

subs
table(subs$type)
```

**Ti/Tv ratio** is one of the first quality checks on any variant call set — genome-wide it should sit near 2, and much lower usually means noise.

---

## Modes of genetic innovation {.scrollable}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p32_1.jpg){height="430px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
1. **Intragenic mutation** — an existing gene is modified by sequence change, mostly through replication error;
2. **Gene duplication** — a gene is duplicated into an initially identical pair, which may then diverge;
3. **Segment shuffling** — two or more genes are broken and rejoined into a hybrid gene;
4. **Horizontal transfer** — DNA moves from one cell's genome to another, even across species, in contrast to the usual vertical transfer from parent to progeny.
:::
:::
:::

---

## DNA replication

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p33_1.jpg){height="380px"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- DNA polymerases copy each of the two strands independently;
- the strands must be unwound at a **replication fork**;
- polymerases **cannot start without a primer** — in cells a short RNA stretch made by a primase, complementary to the template.

![](/assets/code_of_life/p33_2.jpg)
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
"Cannot start without a primer" is the sentence PCR is built on. Everything in the next section is a way of supplying that primer deliberately.
:::

---

# The first molecular toolkit

PCR · melting temperature · electrophoresis · Sanger sequencing

---

## Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

![](/assets/code_of_life/p34_1.jpg){height="330px"}

**Step 1** heat to separate strands → **Step 2** hybridisation of primers → **Step 3** DNA synthesis from primers, with polymerase and dNTPs. Repeat.

---

## Melting temperature (Tm)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p35_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- The temperature at which **50% of the DNA is denatured**;
- G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds, A–T only two;
- critical for **primers** (PCR) and for **probes** (hybridisation).
:::
:::

```{r}
#| label: primer-tm
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

primers <- c(`27F` = "AGAGTTTGATCMTGGCTCAG", `1492R` = "TACGGYTACCTTGTTACGACTT")

data.frame(
  primer = names(primers),
  length = nchar(primers),
  gc_pct = sapply(primers, gc_pct),
  tm_c   = sapply(primers, tm_wallace)   # Wallace rule: 2(A+T) + 4(G+C)
) |> knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Degenerate positions (M, Y) are ignored here — which is exactly why the Wallace rule is a back-of-envelope estimate, not a substitute for a nearest-neighbour calculation.
:::

---

## PCR — exponential in theory

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p36_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p36_2.jpg)

::: {.credit}
Animation: <https://www.gene-quantification.de/pcr-animation.gif>
:::
:::
:::

```{r}
#| label: pcr-copies
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

cycles <- 0:40
data.frame(cycle = cycles, copies = 2^cycles) |> tail(3)
```

2⁴⁰ ≈ **1000 billion copies** — from one template, in about two hours.

## Electrophoresis

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p38_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p38_2.jpg)
:::
:::

An **electrokinetic process** that separates charged particles in a fluid using an electric field — DNA is negatively charged, so it runs to the anode, and shorter molecules run further.

---

## Sanger sequencing (first generation)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p39_1.jpg){height="380px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p39_2.jpg){height="380px"}

**Terminator** nucleotides: a ddNTP has no 3′-OH, so the chain stops when one is incorporated.
:::
:::

## Sanger — the whole workflow

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p40_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p41_1.jpg)
:::

Denature → copy the segment → attach a primer → four polymerase reactions → grow chains to termination → denature → electrophorese and read the ladder.

# Introduction to molecular ecology

From molecules back out to populations

---

## What is molecular ecology? {.scrollable}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
**Ecology** is the scientific study of the distribution and abundance of organisms — the outcome of interactions between individuals (inter- and intraspecific competition) and between organisms and their abiotic environments.

**Molecular ecology** is interdisciplinary: it brings together molecular biology — the study of DNA, RNA, and proteins — and ecology.

::: {.incremental}
- Molecular ecology as we know it did not really exist before the **mid-1980s**;
- the British Ecological Society (founded 1913, the oldest in the world) titled its 1991 conference at the University of East Anglia **"Genes in Ecology"**;
- **1992** — first issue of *Molecular Ecology*;
- **2001** — *Molecular Ecology Resources*.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p43_2.jpg){height="200px"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p43_5.jpg){height="200px"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p43_6.jpg){height="200px"}
:::
:::

---

## The allozyme era

**Allozymes** — proteins differing in electrophoretic mobility as a result of allelic differences in the protein sequence, which ultimately reflect variation in the corresponding DNA sequence.

Population genetics entered the molecular age with two 1966 papers:

- *Drosophila pseudoobscura* — Lewontin & Hubby 1966;
- humans — Harris 1966.

Genetic diversity was measured in two ways:

- **H** — the average proportion of loci heterozygous in an individual (heterozygosity, gene diversity);
- **P** — the average proportion of loci polymorphic in the population (gene polymorphism).

---

## Allozymes and isozymes

::: {.dropdown-table}

<details>
<summary><strong>Allozymes</strong> — variants of the same enzyme, same locus</summary>

Variant forms of an enzyme that differ structurally but **not functionally** from other allozymes coded by different alleles **at the same locus**. Because they differ in structure, they can be separated by electrophoresis.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Isozymes</strong> — same function, different loci</summary>

Enzymes that perform the same function but are coded by genes located at **different loci**.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Why phylogeneticists used them</strong></summary>

Alloenzymes are common biological enzymes showing high functional conservation across phyla and kingdoms, so they were used as **molecular markers** to gauge evolutionary history and relationships between species.

</details>

:::

---

## Losing ground to DNA markers

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p46_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Since the 1960s allozymes played an ongoing role in animal and plant population studies — and then, from the mid-1990s, gave way to DNA markers.

By 2008 they were below 10% of published studies; microsatellites had taken the field.
:::
:::

---

## Relative importance of genotyping strategies

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p47_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **SNP** — single-nucleotide polymorphism;
- **NGS** — next-generation sequencing;
- **FLPs** — fragment length polymorphisms: RFLP, AFLP, microsatellites.
:::
:::

---

## The cost of sequencing

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p48_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
Moore's Law predicts a doubling of computing power every two years. Sequencing cost followed a similar curve — until **2007**, when next-generation sequencing broke away from it entirely.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The break in this curve is why the rest of the course exists: the method stopped being the limiting factor and study design became the limiting factor.
:::

---

## Ribosomal RNA: the tree of life

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p50_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Woese C., Kandler O., Wheelis M. (1990):
*Towards a natural system of organisms: proposal for the domains Archaea, Bacteria, and Eucarya.*
**PNAS** 87 (12) — ~6956 citations.

One conserved gene, present in everything that translates, used to relate everything that lives.
:::
:::

---

## Two domains, not three? {.scrollable}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/code_of_life/p51_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
Williams T. A. *et al.* (2020): *Phylogenomics provides robust support for a two-domains tree of life.* **Nature Ecology & Evolution** 4(1): 138–147.

> "We find that eukaryotes consistently originate from within the archaea in a two-domains tree when due consideration is given to the fit between model and data."

> "Heimdallarchaeota as the current best candidate for the closest archaeal relatives of the eukaryotic nuclear lineage."

::: {.callout-important}
The domain system includes no non-cellular life. In 2012 Stefan Luketa proposed a five-domain system, adding **Prionobiota** (acellular, no nucleic acid) and **Virusobiota** (acellular, with nucleic acid).
:::
:::
:::

---

## Viruses

![](/assets/code_of_life/p52_1.jpg){height="330px"}

**The problem with viruses: two viruses can have nothing in common.** No shared gene, no shared genome chemistry — RNA or DNA, single- or double-stranded, naked or enveloped. There is no 16S for viruses.

---

## Check yourself {.scrollable}

::: {.dropdown-table}

<details>
<summary>Why does a GC-rich primer have a higher Tm?</summary>

Each G–C pair is held by three hydrogen bonds against two for A–T, so more energy — a higher temperature — is needed to separate the strands.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why are transitions more common than transversions, despite being fewer in kind?</summary>

The molecular mechanisms that generate them (notably deamination) favour purine↔purine and pyrimidine↔pyrimidine change; and because of wobble, transitions are more often synonymous, so selection removes fewer of them.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why is 16S rRNA the marker of choice for prokaryote community work?</summary>

It is universal in cellular life, functionally constrained (so it is alignable across enormous distances), ~1600 bp long, and interleaves conserved primer-binding regions with nine variable regions carrying taxonomic signal.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why did allozymes lose to DNA markers?</summary>

Allozymes only see variation that changes protein charge or shape — a small, biased fraction of the variation that exists — and require fresh tissue and enzyme activity. DNA markers see silent variation too, work on degraded and archived material, and scale.

</details>

:::

---

## Key takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- **Base pairing** is chemistry, not convention — and it sets Tm, primer design, and probe specificity;
- **redundancy in the genetic code** makes synonymous sites the neutral clock we later exploit;
- **genome size tells you almost nothing about gene number** — noncoding DNA dominates the difference;
- **regulation** is where the environment enters the molecular story;
- **PCR** exists because polymerases cannot start without a primer;
- **molecular ecology** is ~35 years old, and its markers changed as sequencing cost collapsed;
- **rRNA rewrote the tree of life** — and the two-domain debate shows the tree is still moving.
:::
